reading: Chapter 9, Verification before trust: sections 9.1 to 9.9
intro: In this module you learn to treat everything an agent produces as a hypothesis until it has passed a check. You will see why verification is a family of checks rather than one, the 3 ways it fails in agentic work, and the rule that no output merges without passing a gate. You will also learn how to verify a system with a model inside it, and how to gather the evidence that a change is fit to merge.

ideas.title: Every output is a hypothesis
ideas.text: The agent's report that a task is finished only records that the work looks finished to the agent. Every output stays a hypothesis until it has been checked, and nothing enters the project because it looks finished.

ideas.title: Verification is a category, not a technique
ideas.text: Tests catch wrong behavior, type checks catch values of the wrong kind, linters catch known bad patterns, manual review catches a design that is wrong as a whole, and acceptance gates check the work against the specification. No single check covers all these kinds of fault, so the skill is placing the right check at the right gate.

ideas.title: Tests that confirm the implementation
ideas.text: If an agent writes its tests by reading its own code, the tests check what the code does, not what the specification asked, and they can even defend the fault. Write the tests from the specification, before the code exists or by a different agent that never sees the code.

ideas.title: Verification theatre and the bypassed gate
ideas.text: A gate that catches no real fault is decoration, and it is worse than no gate because it is trusted: a coverage figure only says which lines ran, not what was checked. A gate skipped under pressure protects nothing, so the tools must refuse the merge and the team must hold the rule together.

ideas.title: No gate, no merge
ideas.text: No output enters the main line without passing a gate that was defined in advance and is applied to every change. Cheap automated gates run first and the human gate runs last, so your attention goes only to work that has passed everything a machine can decide.

ideas.title: Verify the code around the model
ideas.text: In a system with a model inside it, you verify the code around the model, not the model's judgment. That code must check the shape of each answer, handle a failed or malformed response instead of passing it on, and store what it keeps correctly. You test this by feeding it bad responses on purpose.

ideas.title: The Merge-Readiness Pack
ideas.text: The pack is the evidence that a change is fit to merge, under 5 headings: functional completeness, sound verification, engineering hygiene, rationale and communication, and full auditability. It turns the reviewer's task from reconstruction into confirmation.

practice.question: An agent writes a median function that is wrong for lists of even length. It then writes tests by running its own function and recording what came back. What is the result?
options: a
The tests fail on even-length lists, so the fault is caught.
b
The type checker catches the fault before the tests run.
c
All tests pass, and a later correct fix would make them fail.
d
Coverage drops, which warns you that a case is missing.
practice.right: Correct. Tests drawn from the implementation do not only miss its fault, they defend it.

practice.question: Your test suite reports 90% coverage. What does that figure tell you?
options: a
That 90% of the code's behavior has been checked against the specification.
b
That 90% of the lines ran while the tests executed, whether or not anything checked them.
c
That the change is safe to merge without a human review.
d
That only 10% of the faults in the code are left to find.
practice.right: Correct. Coverage measures how much code was exercised, not how much behavior was checked.

practice.question: A Tribunal judge returns 3 paragraphs of reasoning but never says justified or not justified. What should the code around the judge do?
options: a
Treat the response as a failure, then retry the call or record that it could not be completed.
b
Store the reasoning in the protocol, since the model did answer.
c
Guess the verdict from the tone of the reasoning and store it.
d
Leave it alone, because the model's judgment is a matter of product evaluation.
practice.right: Correct. A malformed answer is never stored as though it were a verdict.

practice.question: Why should the gate be defined before the work it judges?
options: a
Because automated gates cannot be changed once the pipeline runs.
b
Because the agent needs the gate in its context to write correct code.
c
Because a gate defined first is cheaper to run.
d
Because a standard invented after the work bends to fit the work instead of judging it.
practice.right: Correct. A gate designed around the first change it meets is designed to let that change through.

practice.question: An agent rewrote the function that rounds invoice totals. The type checker and the linter passed, the agent's own tests (written after the code) passed, and the change was merged within the hour without anyone reading it or comparing it with the specification. Which members of the verification family were applied, which were not, and what kind of fault did each missing member leave unchecked?
practice.help: Write your own answer first, then compare it with the teacher's answer.
practice.model: Type checks and linters were applied, and tests were applied only in a weak form, because the agent wrote them from its own code. So wrong behavior against the specification was not really checked: the tests can only show that the code agrees with itself. Manual review was not applied, so a design that is wrong as a whole, such as rounding at the wrong step, was left unchecked. The acceptance gate was not applied either, so nobody checked whether the function does what the specification asked.

practice.question: Write the acceptance criteria for one feature of your own project, or of the Tribunal, directly from its specification. Mark each criterion as checkable automatically or needing a human reading, and say why at least one must be read by a person.
practice.help: Write your own answer first, then compare it with the teacher's answer.
practice.model: For the Tribunal judges: each stored verdict is exactly justified or not justified (automatic); each verdict has at least 2 reasons (automatic); a malformed or empty response is never stored as a verdict (automatic, with a stub that feeds bad responses). The reasons are drawn from the charge sheet and not invented, and each judge's reasoning is recognizably its own rather than generic (human reading). These last ones cannot be tested by any machine, so an engineer reads and signs for them as the human part of the gate. A specification whose every criterion can be automated has probably not stated the ones that matter.
